claim: A gene fusion encoding ribosomal protein S16 linked via its C-terminus to the biotinylation domain of the biotin carboxyl carrier protein (BCCP) was introduced into the chromosome of Escherichia coli.
source: A gene fusion encoding ribosomal protein S16 linked via its C-terminus to the biotinylation domain of the biotin carboxyl carrier protein (BCCP) was introduced (Link et al., 1997) into the chromosome of Escherichia coli, and biotinylated ribosomes were then purified.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Link et al., 1997, indicating this method was previously established and applied in this study.

claim: Biotinylated ribosomes were purified from E. coli expressing the S16-BCCP fusion.
source: A gene fusion encoding ribosomal protein S16 linked via its C-terminus to the biotinylation domain of the biotin carboxyl carrier protein (BCCP) was introduced (Link et al., 1997) into the chromosome of Escherichia coli, and biotinylated ribosomes were then purified.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental procedure of purifying biotinylated ribosomes.

claim: No translation signals were detected in the absence of GTP.
source: No translation signals were detected in the absence of GTP and EF-G. (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F, which are control experiments.

claim: No translation signals were detected in the absence of EF-G.
source: No translation signals were detected in the absence of GTP and EF-G. (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E,F, which are control experiments.

claim: Ribosomes do not translate the message in a continuous manner, but in bursts of translation separated by long pauses.
source: Ribosomes do not translate the message in a continuous manner, but in bursts of translation separated by long pauses (Figure 1B) that do not appear to be correlated with template position.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Translation pauses do not appear to be correlated with template position.
source: Ribosomes do not translate the message in a continuous manner, but in bursts of translation separated by long pauses (Figure 1B) that do not appear to be correlated with template position.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Some trajectories observed during translation bursts exhibit a particularly low noise level and clearly show that the ribosome moves in periods of stationary dwells followed by translocation events corresponding to single codon steps (three nucleotides) along the mRNA.
source: As a result, some of the trajectories observed during translation bursts exhibit a particularly low noise level, and clearly show that the ribosome moves in periods of stationary dwells that are followed by translocation events corresponding to single codon steps (three nucleotides) along the mRNA (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation in experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: As the opposing force is increased, the mean pause-free velocity decreases monotonically.
source: We find that as the opposing force, F, is increased, the mean pause-free velocity, v, decreases monotonically (Figure 2), indicating that mRNA translocation is rate limiting under the conditions of the experiment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: mRNA translocation is rate limiting under the conditions of the experiment.
source: We find that as the opposing force, F, is increased, the mean pause-free velocity, v, decreases monotonically (Figure 2), indicating that mRNA translocation is rate limiting under the conditions of the experiment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that velocity decreases with increasing force, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The applied force acts between the 3′ end of the mRNA and the small 30S subunit.
source: Note that the applied force acts between the 3′ end of the mRNA and the small 30S subunit; there is no directly applied force between the mRNA and the large 50S subunit or between the 30S and the 50S subunits.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental geometry and how force is applied in the assay.

claim: There is no directly applied force between the mRNA and the large 50S subunit.

evidence: The claim describes the experimental geometry and how force is applied in the assay.

claim: There is no directly applied force between the 30S and the 50S subunits.

evidence: The claim describes the experimental geometry and how force is applied in the assay.

claim: The position of the attachment point (protein S16, in the 'back' of the 30S subunit) was chosen because it is remote of any known functional site and is not known to exhibit conformational dynamics during translocation.
source: In addition, the position of the attachment point (protein S16, in the 'back' of the 30S subunit) was chosen because it is remote of any known functional site and is not known to exhibit conformational dynamics during translocation.

claim: Force only affects directly the mechanical step in which the anticodon loops of the tRNAs move from the A and P sites to the canonical P and E sites of the 30S subunit, respectively, together with the concomitant movement of the mRNA with respect to the ribosome.
source: As a result, force only affects directly the mechanical step in which the anticodon loops of the tRNAs move from the A and P sites to the canonical P and E sites of the 30S subunit, respectively, together with the concomitant movement of the mRNA with respect to the ribosome.

claim: The zero-force velocity v0 = 2.9 codons/s (1.8, 4.0).
source: The fit yields a zero-force velocity v0 = 2.9 codons/s (1.8, 4.0) and a distance x˜ = 1.4 nm (0.9, 1.8).
evidence: The claim is derived from fitting experimental data to an Arrhenius expression.

claim: The characteristic distance x˜ = 1.4 nm (0.9, 1.8).

evidence: The claim is derived from fitting experimental data to an Arrhenius expression.

claim: Crystal structures show that the distance between A- and P-site mRNA codons equals 1.48 nm.
source: Notably, these results have implications for the intrinsic step size during translocation: crystal structures (Jenner et al., 2010) show that the distance between A- and P-site mRNA codons equals 1.48 nm.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to crystal structure data from Jenner et al., 2010.

claim: The ribosome likely functions as a Brownian ratchet during translocation.
source: While these are two idealized cases and a real system is likely to combine features of these two models, the distance determined here (1.4 nm) is very close to the full 1.48 nm step size and indicates that, while we cannot fully rule out a PS mechanism, the ribosome likely functions as a BR during translocation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of the measured distance to theoretical predictions for different mechanisms.

claim: The ribosome can generate forces as high as 13 ± 2 pN.
source: Our results indicate that the ribosome can generate forces as high as 13 ± 2 pN.
evidence: The claim is derived from experimental measurements of the stall force.

claim: The ribosome stall force is very close to that required to unwind the strongest secondary structure motifs typically present in mRNA.
source: Remarkably, the ribosome stall force is very close to that required to unwind the strongest secondary structure motifs typically present in mRNA (Tinoco et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim compares the measured stall force to known values for RNA secondary structure stability, supported by citation to Tinoco et al., 2004.

claim: The comparable magnitude between the mechanical strengths of RNAs and the stall force of the ribosome indicates that RNA secondary structures can have a strong effect on the rate of translation.
source: The comparable magnitude between the mechanical strengths of RNAs and the stall force of the ribosome indicates that RNA secondary structures can have a strong effect on the rate of translation (and hence on phenomena such as frameshifting and cotranslational folding of the protein) and explains how these structures, while not being insurmountable barriers, can fulfill a regulatory role in the cell.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of measured stall force to RNA stability.

claim: RNA secondary structures can fulfill a regulatory role in the cell.
source: The comparable magnitude between the mechanical strengths of RNAs and the stall force of the ribosome indicates that RNA secondary structures can have a strong effect on the rate of translation (and hence on phenomena such as frameshifting and cotranslational folding of the protein) and explains how these structures, while not being insurmountable barriers, can fulfill a regulatory role in the cell.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of measured stall force to RNA stability.

claim: The work generated by the ribosome near stalling is 21.2 pN · nm = 5.2 kBT or about 3.1 Kcal/mol.
source: The work generated by the ribosome near stalling, that is, the product of the stall force and the step size, 21.2 pN · nm = 5.2 kBT or about 3.1 Kcal/mol, represents the maximal mechanical work generated by the motor during the translocation step.
evidence: The claim is calculated from the measured stall force and step size.

claim: The free-energy difference between peptide bond and ester bond hydrolysis is approximately −3.7 ± 1.2 kcal/mol, equivalent to 6.3 ± 2 kBT per bond exchange in the experimental conditions.
source: The free-energy difference between peptide bond and ester bond hydrolysis is approximately −3.7 ± 1.2 kcal/mol, equivalent to 6.3 ± 2 kBT per bond exchange in our experimental conditions ('Materials and methods').
evidence: The claim is calculated from thermodynamic data provided in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The maximal mechanical work that can be generated by the ribosome is ∼80% of the total energy available from transpeptidation.
source: Hence, the maximal mechanical work that can be generated by the ribosome is ∼80% of the total energy available from transpeptidation and, in principle, it is possible to power translocation from this energy without the need to invoke an energetic contribution from the hydrolysis of GTP.
evidence: The claim is calculated from the measured mechanical work and the free energy of transpeptidation.

claim: In principle, it is possible to power translocation from the energy of transpeptidation without the need to invoke an energetic contribution from the hydrolysis of GTP.
source: Hence, the maximal mechanical work that can be generated by the ribosome is ∼80% of the total energy available from transpeptidation and, in principle, it is possible to power translocation from this energy without the need to invoke an energetic contribution from the hydrolysis of GTP.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on thermodynamic calculations.

claim: Studies have shown that the ribosome can translocate in the absence of EF-G.
source: In fact, studies have shown that the ribosome can translocate in the absence of EF-G (Gavrilova et al., 1976) or in the absence of GTP (Pestka, 1969; Rodnina et al., 1997; Fredrick and Noller, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies have shown that the ribosome can translocate in the absence of GTP.
source: In fact, studies have shown that the ribosome can translocate in the absence of EF-G (Gavrilova et al., 1976) or in the absence of GTP (Pestka, 1969; Rodnina et al., 1997; Fredrick and Noller, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous forward translocation is unfavorable in many contexts.
source: However, spontaneous forward translocation is unfavorable in many contexts (Shoji et al., 2006), and efficient and rapid translocation does require EF-G and GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shoji et al., 2006.

claim: Efficient and rapid translocation does require EF-G and GTP hydrolysis.
source: However, spontaneous forward translocation is unfavorable in many contexts (Shoji et al., 2006), and efficient and rapid translocation does require EF-G and GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and cited literature.

claim: 80% thermodynamic efficiency for conversion of chemical energy to mechanical motion is higher than occurs in most molecular motors.
source: Furthermore, 80% thermodynamic efficiency for conversion of chemical energy to mechanical motion is higher than occurs in most molecular motors (Bustamante et al., 2004), and, moreover, it is not clear how the energy available from peptide bond formation could be stored and transmitted from the 50S to the 30S subunit.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bustamante et al., 2004 and general knowledge about molecular motors.

claim: It is not clear how the energy available from peptide bond formation could be stored and transmitted from the 50S to the 30S subunit.
source: Furthermore, 80% thermodynamic efficiency for conversion of chemical energy to mechanical motion is higher than occurs in most molecular motors (Bustamante et al., 2004), and, moreover, it is not clear how the energy available from peptide bond formation could be stored and transmitted from the 50S to the 30S subunit.
evidence: The claim represents a gap in understanding and is speculative.

claim: A mechanism in which EF-G binding and GTP hydrolysis account for the energy of translocation and resetting (including EF-G–GDP dissociation) appears to be more likely.
source: Instead, in view of our results, a mechanism in which EF-G binding and GTP hydrolysis account for the energy of translocation and resetting (including EF-G–GDP dissociation) appears to be more likely.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and thermodynamic considerations.

claim: The duration of the translation bursts (and hence the effective pause entry rate, kp) is independent of the force opposing translocation.
source: The duration of the translation bursts (and hence the effective pause entry rate, kp) is independent of the force opposing translocation (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The full distribution of burst durations is well described, at all forces, by a single exponential function with nearly identical parameters.
source: Moreover, the full distribution of burst durations is well described, at all forces, by a single exponential function with nearly identical parameters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The duration of the pauses (and hence the pause exit rate, k-p) is independent of force.
source: Likewise, Figure 4B shows that the duration of the pauses (and hence the pause exit rate, k-p) is independent of force.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The pause duration is well described by single exponential functions with the same parameters at all the tested forces.
source: Since the pause duration is also well described by single exponential functions with the same parameters at all the tested forces (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we conclude that entering into the paused state and exiting from it are both governed by single, force-independent steps.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Entering into the paused state and exiting from it are both governed by single, force-independent steps.
source: Since the pause duration is also well described by single exponential functions with the same parameters at all the tested forces (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we conclude that entering into the paused state and exiting from it are both governed by single, force-independent steps.

claim: The pause entry rate kp = 0.16 s−1 (0.14, 0.18).
source: Hence, we can cluster all our measurements into one data set and calculate the entry and exit rates: kp = 0.16 s−1 (0.14, 0.18) and k−p = 0.14 s−1 (0.1, 0.18), where the numbers in parenthesis indicate 95% confidence intervals.
evidence: The claim is calculated from experimental data.

claim: The pause exit rate k−p = 0.14 s−1 (0.1, 0.18).
source: Hence, we can cluster all our measurements into one data set and calculate the entry and exit rates: kp = 0.16 s−1 (0.14, 0.18) and k−p = 0.14 s−1 (0.1, 0.18), where the numbers in parenthesis indicate 95% confidence intervals.

claim: The force independence of the entry and exit rates rules out the possibility that pauses are caused by secondary structure motifs.
source: Thus, the force independence of the entry and exit rates rules out this possibility.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that pause rates are force-independent.

claim: The pauses represent events that are off-pathway from the main incorporation and translocation cycle.
source: Hence, we favor a model in which these pauses represent events that are off-pathway from the main incorporation and translocation cycle.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the experimental observations.

claim: The rate limiting transitions into these off-pathway states are steps along a non-mechanical reaction coordinate, or alternatively a mechanical coordinate that is orthogonal to the translocation movement.
source: The rate limiting transitions into these off-pathway states are steps along a non-mechanical reaction coordinate, or alternatively a mechanical coordinate that is orthogonal to the translocation movement, and hence not affected by the externally applied force.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the force-independence of pause rates.

claim: In the conditions of the experiments, the time spent by the ribosome in the productive translation states and the unproductive paused state are nearly the same.
source: Interestingly, the pause entry and exit rates are very similar, indicating that in the conditions of our experiments the time spent by the ribosome in the productive translation states and the unproductive paused state are nearly the same.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity of pause entry and exit rates.

claim: The ribosome possesses three binding sites for tRNA: the aminoacyl (A), peptidyl (P), and exit (E) sites.
source: Ribosomes possess three binding sites for tRNA: the aminoacyl (A), peptidyl (P), and exit (E) sites, each of which is shared between the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ribosome structure.

claim: Each tRNA binding site is shared between the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits.
source: Ribosomes possess three binding sites for tRNA: the aminoacyl (A), peptidyl (P), and exit (E) sites, each of which is shared between the 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ribosome structure.

claim: Following codon recognition and peptide bond formation, the ribosome has a deacylated tRNA in the P site and a peptidyl-tRNA in the A site.
source: Following codon recognition and peptide bond formation, the ribosome has a deacylated tRNA in the P site and a peptidyl-tRNA in the A site.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the translation cycle.

claim: The movement of tRNAs and mRNA relative to the ribosome occurs in two steps.
source: This movement occurs in two steps (Moazed and Noller, 1989b): first, the 3′ ends of the tRNAs in the A and P sites move, with respect to the 50S subunit, into hybrid A/P and P/E states, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moazed and Noller, 1989b.

claim: In the first step of translocation, the 3′ ends of the tRNAs in the A and P sites move, with respect to the 50S subunit, into hybrid A/P and P/E states, respectively.
source: This movement occurs in two steps (Moazed and Noller, 1989b): first, the 3′ ends of the tRNAs in the A and P sites move, with respect to the 50S subunit, into hybrid A/P and P/E states, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moazed and Noller, 1989b.

claim: Formation of hybrid states can occur spontaneously, reversibly, and independently of elongation factor G (EF-G) in vitro.
source: In vitro, formation of these states can occur spontaneously, reversibly, and independently of elongation factor G (EF-G) (Moazed and Noller, 1989b; Sharma et al., 2004; Cornish et al., 2008; Munro et al., 2010) and is coupled to rotation of the 30S body (Moazed and Noller, 1989b; Frank and Agrawal, 2000; Agirrezabala et al., 2008; Julian et al., 2008; Dunkle et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Formation of hybrid states is coupled to rotation of the 30S body.
source: In vitro, formation of these states can occur spontaneously, reversibly, and independently of elongation factor G (EF-G) (Moazed and Noller, 1989b; Sharma et al., 2004; Cornish et al., 2008; Munro et al., 2010) and is coupled to rotation of the 30S body (Moazed and Noller, 1989b; Frank and Agrawal, 2000; Agirrezabala et al., 2008; Julian et al., 2008; Dunkle et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The second step of translocation is irreversible and EF-G-dependent.
source: In the second step, which is irreversible and EF-G-dependent (Moazed and Noller, 1989b; Savelsbergh et al., 2003), the mRNA is translocated by one codon, along with movement of the associated anticodon ends of the tRNAs to the classical P and E sites, coupled to an orthogonal rotation of the 30S subunit head domain (Ratje et al., 2010; Dunkle et al., 2011; Ermolenko and Noller, 2011; Guo and Noller, 2012; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the second step, the mRNA is translocated by one codon, along with movement of the associated anticodon ends of the tRNAs to the classical P and E sites.
source: In the second step, which is irreversible and EF-G-dependent (Moazed and Noller, 1989b; Savelsbergh et al., 2003), the mRNA is translocated by one codon, along with movement of the associated anticodon ends of the tRNAs to the classical P and E sites, coupled to an orthogonal rotation of the 30S subunit head domain (Ratje et al., 2010; Dunkle et al., 2011; Ermolenko and Noller, 2011; Guo and Noller, 2012; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The second step of translocation is coupled to an orthogonal rotation of the 30S subunit head domain.

claim: The translocation process involves reverse rotational movements of the 30S subunit body and head.
source: The translocation process also involves other large-scale conformational changes in the ribosome, including reverse rotational movements of the 30S subunit body and head (Ermolenko and Noller, 2011; Guo and Noller, 2012), and movement of the large subunit L1 stalk into the intersubunit space (Fei et al., 2008; Cornish et al., 2009).

claim: The translocation process involves movement of the large subunit L1 stalk into the intersubunit space.
source: The translocation process also involves other large-scale conformational changes in the ribosome, including reverse rotational movements of the 30S subunit body and head (Ermolenko and Noller, 2011; Guo and Noller, 2012), and movement of the large subunit L1 stalk into the intersubunit space (Fei et al., 2008; Cornish et al., 2009).

claim: Translocation is a highly coordinated and complex process composed of inter- and intra-molecular, force-generating mechanical movements.
source: Translocation is therefore a highly coordinated and complex process composed of inter- and intra-molecular, force-generating mechanical movements.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on the described conformational changes.

claim: During translation, the ribosome must overcome significant mechanical barriers posed by structured portions of the mRNA.
source: During translation, the ribosome must also overcome significant mechanical barriers posed by structured portions of the mRNA.

claim: Pseudoknots and hairpins are used to induce programmed frameshifting.
source: These structures are exploited by the cell to create diverse strategies for translation regulation; for example, pseudoknots and hairpins are used to induce programmed frameshifting (Tsuchihashi, 1991; Namy et al., 2006), whereas synonymous mutations that can alter the local structure of RNA and codon usage are employed to control protein expression levels (Duan et al., 2003; Nackley et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Synonymous mutations that can alter the local structure of RNA and codon usage are employed to control protein expression levels.
source: These structures are exploited by the cell to create diverse strategies for translation regulation; for example, pseudoknots and hairpins are used to induce programmed frameshifting (Tsuchihashi, 1991; Namy et al., 2006), whereas synonymous mutations that can alter the local structure of RNA and codon usage are employed to control protein expression levels (Duan et al., 2003; Nackley et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Force is not only a product of the chemical reactions during translation, but also an important player in the regulation of this process.
source: Hence, force is not only a product of the chemical reactions during translation, but also an important player in the regulation of this process.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discussion of mRNA structures and their regulatory roles.

claim: Recent crystallographic studies of the ribosome bound to EF-G in a translocation intermediate can lend support for the Brownian ratchet mechanism.
source: Notably, recent crystallographic studies of the ribosome bound to EF-G in a translocation intermediate (Chen et al., 2013; Pulk and Cate, 2013; Tourigny et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013), and a previous structure of the ribosome bound to EF-G in the post-translocation state (Gao et al., 2009) can lend support for this result and help clarify the identity of the reaction that rectifies translocation in this ratchet mechanism
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent crystallographic studies.
